claims.text: Controlled boron doping of a tungsten-rich high-entropy alloy will promote in situ formation of tungsten-boride precipitates.
The tungsten-boride precipitates will form a uniformly fine network along grain boundaries.
The tungsten-boride network will reduce thermal resistance and improve heat-transfer capability.
The proposed improvement in heat transfer will occur without compromising mechanical integrity under plasma-facing reactor conditions.
The initial powder-metallurgy tungsten-rich alloy has a conventional microstructure lacking secondary-phase precipitates.
Boron addition through SHS followed by SPS can be optimized to produce fine, uniformly distributed tungsten-boride precipitates.
Tungsten-boride precipitates act as high-thermal-conductivity bridges across grain boundaries.
The proposed bridging effect lowers intergranular thermal resistance.
Grain-boundary pinning inhibits grain growth under cyclic high-temperature loading.
Inhibition of grain growth preserves the alloy's mechanical stability under cyclic loading.
The optimized boron-doped alloy will have lower thermal resistance than an otherwise equivalently processed undoped alloy.
The optimized boron-doped alloy will maintain or enhance mechanical integrity relative to the undoped alloy during high-temperature thermal cycling and mechanical stress.
The proposed benefits will persist at temperatures up to 900 degrees Celsius under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.
Boron concentrations above the optimum or poorly controlled processing may cause precipitate coarsening.
Coarsened precipitates may cause embrittlement and compromise mechanical integrity.
